claims.text: Most of the time the human in the loop, or the agent in the same place, is asked for a yes or a no, which is the least interesting part of a decision.
claims.quote: is asked for a yes or a no, and that is the least interesting part of a decision

claims.text: Agency has seven dimensions, options, context, depth, time, incentives, escalation and authority, each observable at the decision point, and the weakest one caps the decision.
claims.quote: options, context, depth, time, incentives, escalation and authority

claims.text: The dimensions become a scale of seven levels from the rubber stamp to the delegator, and the vault scores fourteen cases from the record and from the owner's own agent team.
claims.quote: scores fourteen cases from the record and from my own agent team

value.unit: decision points scored on the scale

claims.text: Below level 3 the decider holds the liability for a decision the system made, and accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point and up their chain.
claims.quote: Below level 3, the decider holds the liability for a decision the system made

claims.text: The owner is a human in the loop: agents prepare emails daily and none sends on its own, except a security agent that may send one email to one address to put the team on hold.
claims.quote: a security agent may send one email, to one address, to put the team on hold

claims.text: A no stalls the work and makes somebody a problem, so yes is always tempting; a decider whose only realistic answer is yes has no agency at all.
claims.quote: A decider whose only realistic answer is yes has, in practice, no agency at all.

claims.text: The record has a prompt that asked to add a repository without saying why, a vendor reporting that its users approve 93% of permission prompts, and a sign-in push accepted after enough repetitions.
claims.quote: a vendor reporting that its users approve 93% of permission prompts

value.unit: percent of permission prompts approved, one vendor's report

claims.text: A prompt that asked to add label 756-459-3214 could be neither a good nor a bad decision; it was a click.
claims.quote: There was no way for that decision to be a good one, and no way for it to be a bad one either; it was a click.

claims.text: Whatever you punish, you teach the other answer: a reviewer blamed only for approvals says no, one punished for delay says yes; Ritov and Baron called the underlying effect omission bias in 1990.
claims.quote: Whatever you punish, you teach the other answer.

claims.text: Agency needs incentives that treat a wrong yes and a wrong no alike, a margin for honest error, time, and somewhere to escalate.
claims.quote: agency needs incentives that treat a wrong yes and a wrong no alike, and a margin for honest error

claims.text: Everything a decider is shown is a compression of reality, and provenance and fractal semantic graphs are what let them zoom from the summary to the claim to the source.
claims.quote: Every time we look at something, we are looking at a compression of reality

claims.text: In Eriksson and Stanton's simulator study, drivers took between 1.9 and 25.7 seconds to take back control from an automated vehicle in non-critical conditions.
claims.quote: drivers took between 1.9 and 25.7 seconds to take back control in non-critical conditions

value.unit: seconds to take back control, upper bound

claims.text: Lisanne Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation, 1983: the more advanced a control system, the more crucial the human operator's contribution, and the less ready the human is for it.
claims.quote: the more advanced a control system is, so the more crucial may be the contribution of the human operator

claims.text: The record of blame is the moral crumple zone and the Post Office's sub-postmasters, held to shortfalls they could not dispute; European guidance says sign-off must be meaningful rather than a token gesture.
claims.quote: the Post Office's sub-postmasters, held to shortfalls they had no way of disputing

claims.text: When a person in the loop has no agency, responsibility should sit with whoever designed the decision point, their boss and their boss's boss, who authorised a system that will statistically make mistakes.
claims.quote: It should sit with whoever designed the decision point, and their boss, and their boss's boss

claims.text: Each dimension's answer caps the level and the level is the lowest cap: context without time is still a guess, time without authority still a sign-off.
claims.quote: one weak dimension caps the whole decision, the way one weak link caps a chain

claims.text: Eight of the fourteen cases sit at level 0, the fixed sign-in push reaches level 1, a senior clinician at the end of an escalation chain is at level 4, the owner's draft review at 5, and the security agent's one email at 6.
claims.quote: Eight of them sit at level 0, including the label prompt

value.unit: cases at level 0, the rubber stamp

claims.text: The scale does not care whether the decider is a person: an agent asked whether a draft is fine to send with no record, budget or escalation is a rubber stamp, and the Hope or enforcement controller is at level 3.
claims.quote: with the draft and nothing else, no tools to check the record, no budget and nowhere to escalate, is a rubber stamp

claims.text: The final decision should not be an agent's but code, a decision tree of checks each of which can be followed and questioned; models prepare and propose, rules decide, people own the rules.
claims.quote: Models prepare and propose; rules decide; people own the rules.

claims.text: Above level 3 a review is QA, not a sign-off: the useful question is how we got here, and the right fix is to the record, the graph or the objectives rather than the email.
claims.quote: The right fix is not to the email. It is to the record, the graph, the connection

claims.text: Every time someone with context fixes the source they validate many earlier decisions and the graph gets more granular; the owner reads everything that comes back, which is how he learns which workflows work.
claims.quote: I read it all, and it is how I learn which workflows work.

claims.text: Ownership makes engagement: a policy published under a stakeholder's name, a risk accepted in writing, an email that goes out under the owner's name.
claims.quote: until someone has to accept a risk in writing, they do not really engage

claims.text: The agent team labels each draft for review or ready to send, and an agent can write a draft with no recipient carrying its questions, a small interface made of an email.
claims.quote: a small interface, made of an email, that the agent then replaces with the real one

claims.text: As drafts of one kind keep coming back correct, the behaviour policy changes to allow that agent in that setup to send that kind of email and nothing else, so the proven cases become rules.
claims.quote: the behaviour policy changes to allow that agent, in that setup, to send that kind of email, and nothing else

claims.text: The smaller models, Anthropic's Sonnet and Haiku in their 5.5 versions, reason well enough for well-defined tasks, and the person reviewing what remains should be the most senior and most time-pressed.
claims.quote: now reason well enough for tasks that are well defined

claims.text: The EU AI Act's Articles 14(4) and 26(2), on understanding, overriding and the competence and authority of overseers, read against the scale put the floor at level 3.
claims.quote: Read against the scale, that is a floor at level 3.

claims.text: This has little to do with AI: people have always made decisions they could not explain, and automating a flow without explainability makes the old problem bigger.
claims.quote: automating a flow without explainability makes the old problem bigger

claims.text: Where to start: list the decision points, find the weakest dimension of each, replace identifiers with things, make why answerable, check the incentives, move accountability below level 3, treat review as QA, and turn clean passes into rules.
claims.quote: Find the weakest dimension of each. That is the only one worth fixing first.

claims.text: Two of the fourteen cases are from the author's own agent team; the public-record cases are summarised and sourced in the vault and in Where is the why.
claims.quote: Two cases are from the author's own agent team.

claims.text: How strong omission bias is has been debated since Ritov and Baron named it.
claims.quote: though how strong the effect is has been debated since

claims.text: The article was drafted from two voice memos by Dinis Cruz by agent@riskmandate.ai running Claude Opus 5.5 on 8 October 2026.
claims.quote: Drafted from two voice memos by Dinis Cruz
